figures.caption: FIG. 1. Encoding birdsong syllables into ultra-sparse spike sequences. (a) Overlapping windows (dashed boxes) slide along the spectrogram of a Bengalese finch syllable (top). Each window is a feature vector, i.e., a point in feature space. The syllable traces out a trajectory (bottom). (b) Feature vectors from the same part of one syllable type (filled circles) lie close together in the feature space and occupy a volume (gray) that can be separated from feature vectors of other syllable types (open circles). A feature neuron learns the boundary of this volume. (c) Responses of two feature neurons (right) to continuous song (top). Left: the trajectories of the two syllables and the decision boundaries (gray) of the two neurons. When the trajectory enters the decision boundary, the response crosses a threshold (dashed lines) and the neuron fires an onset spike (green); when it leaves, the response falls below threshold and the neuron fires an offset spike (red). A sustained feature produces a plateau in the response (bottom). (d) A chain of decision boundaries, one per feature neuron, covers the entire trajectory of a syllable; the traces show the responses of the corresponding feature neurons. The syllable is thus represented as a sequence of discrete events. (e) Onset (green) and offset (red) spikes of feature neurons evoked by an isolated syllable. (f) Onset and offset spikes of the feature-neuron population evoked by a continuous song. Green and red dotted lines mark the syllable onsets and offsets determined from the spectrogram. (g) Onset and offset spikes of 5 feature neurons evoked by 7 renditions of the song segment marked by the gray bar in (f). The spikes are reliable and temporally precise.

FIG. 2. Segmenting and classifying syllables in a continuous recording using delay lines. (a) Principle of delay-line template matching. Left: a template in which neurons 1–3 spike at times t1, t2, and t3. Middle: the neurons project to neuron 4 with delays τ1, τ2, and τ3. Right: the delays compensate for the differences in spike times, so the spikes arrive at neuron 4 simultaneously (t1 + τ1 = t2 + τ2 = t3 + τ3) and are easily detected. (b) Separate delay lines carry the onset (green) and offset (red) spikes of feature neurons to an ON and an OFF template neuron. (c) The synchronized spikes (left) are convolved with a Gaussian kernel to tolerate timing jitter and filtered with learned weights (color map), so that reliably firing feature neurons contribute more (right). (d) The weighted onsets and offsets (top) are summed into ON and OFF traces (bottom); ON and OFF spikes are emitted at peaks (arrows) above threshold (dotted lines). (e) Example for one syllable: spectrogram (top), onset (green) and offset (red) spikes of feature neurons (2nd panel), the same spikes after the delay lines (3rd panel), and the resulting ON and OFF spikes (bottom). (f) A continuous song (top) and the ON (green) and OFF (red) spikes of all template neurons, ordered by neuron ID, of a system trained on N = 15 syllables per type (middle). Green and red dotted lines mark the syllable onsets and offsets determined from the spectrogram. Pairing ON and OFF spikes yields the segmentation (bottom): each bar is a predicted syllable, labeled a–s and shaded by its score.

FIG. 4. Continuous recognition of birdsong syllables on the CPU. (a), (b) Recognition results for two benchmarks: 8 Bengalese finches from this paper (a) and 11 Bengalese finches from the uncurated dataset of Ref. [27] (b). Left: word error rates (WERs) versus the number of training syllables per type (5, 10, 20, or 40). Each line is one bird; each point is the average over 10 systems trained on independently sampled training sets (see Appendix A10). Inset: total number of test syllables. Right: total number of training syllables (top) and their total duration in seconds (bottom). Bars show mean ± SD across birds (dots). (c) Examples of recognition output for a bird from benchmark (a) (top) and from benchmark (b) (bottom). Green and red lines mark the start and stop of each recognized syllable, and the labels above give the recognized syllable types.

TABLE I. Dataset IDs, number of syllable types, test set sizes, and number of syllables available for training. Recording files were divided into a test set (60%) and a training pool (40%) from which training sets were drawn. All test syllables were used in the benchmarks. The first eight birds are from this study, while the remaining eleven are from Ref. [27].

FIG. 6. Full diagram of the spiking neural network implemented on the Loihi chip. Inhibitory connections are shown in orange. Excitatory connections are shown in black. Template onset and offset delay lines are shown in green and red, respectively.
